questions.question_text: In his work "A Theory of Justice" (1971), John Rawls argues that the Difference Principle permits social and economic inequalities only if they:
questions.option_a: Maximize aggregate utility across the entire population regardless of distribution
questions.option_b: Work to the greatest benefit of the least-advantaged members of society
questions.option_c: Reward individuals strictly in proportion to aristocratic merit and lineage
questions.option_d: Eliminate all private ownership of productive assets through state nationalization
questions.explanation: John Rawls’s Second Principle of Justice includes the Difference Principle, which holds that inequalities are justifiable only if they are attached to offices open to all under fair equality of opportunity and work to the maximum benefit of the least-advantaged members of society.

questions.question_text: Which Constitutional Amendment Act inserted Article 21A into the Constitution of India, making free and compulsory education a Fundamental Right for children aged 6 to 14 years?
questions.explanation: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A, establishing the Right to Education as a Fundamental Right for children between 6 and 14 years of age.

questions.question_text: Kenneth Waltz’s "Theory of International Politics" (1979) is the foundational text of which school of International Relations?
questions.explanation: Kenneth Waltz pioneered Structural Realism (Neorealism) in his 1979 work, explaining international outcomes through the anarchic structure of the international system and the distribution of capabilities across states rather than human nature.

questions.question_text: Who among the following Indian thinkers authored "The Annihilation of Caste" (1936) and argued that political reform cannot succeed without social reform?
questions.explanation: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar wrote "Annihilation of Caste" in 1936 as an undelivered presidential address to the Jat-Pat-Todak Mandal of Lahore, demonstrating that political democracy requires the destruction of the graded inequality of caste.

questions.question_text: According to Isaiah Berlin in "Two Concepts of Liberty" (1958), negative liberty primarily refers to:
questions.option_a: Collective self-realization through obedience to the general will of the state
questions.option_b: The area within which a subject is left to do or be what they are able to do or be, without interference by others
questions.option_c: State-mandated redistribution of material wealth to guarantee identical outcomes
questions.option_d: Active participation in deliberative assemblies of the ancient polis
questions.explanation: Isaiah Berlin distinguished negative liberty ("freedom from external interference or coercion") from positive liberty ("freedom as self-mastery and rational self-direction").

questions.question_text: In Kautilya’s Arthashastra, the Saptanga Theory of the State enumerates seven constituent elements (Prakritis). Which element is identified as the "Janapada"?
questions.explanation: The seven limbs (Saptanga) in Kautilya’s Arthashastra are Swami (Ruler), Amatya (Minister), Janapada (Territory & Population), Durga (Fortified Capital), Kosha (Treasury), Danda (Army/Force), and Mitra (Ally).

questions.question_text: Kenneth Waltz’s "Theory of International Politics" (1979) is the foundational text of which school of International Relations?
questions.explanation: Kenneth Waltz pioneered Structural Realism (Neorealism) in his 1979 work, explaining international outcomes through the anarchic structure of the international system and the distribution of capabilities across states rather than human nature.

questions.question_text: Who among the following Indian thinkers authored "The Annihilation of Caste" (1936) and argued that political reform cannot succeed without social reform?
questions.explanation: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar wrote "Annihilation of Caste" in 1936 as an undelivered presidential address to the Jat-Pat-Todak Mandal of Lahore, demonstrating that political democracy requires the destruction of the graded inequality of caste.

questions.question_text: According to Isaiah Berlin in "Two Concepts of Liberty" (1958), negative liberty primarily refers to:
questions.option_a: Collective self-realization through obedience to the general will of the state
questions.option_b: The area within which a subject is left to do or be what they are able to do or be, without interference by others
questions.option_c: State-mandated redistribution of material wealth to guarantee identical outcomes
questions.option_d: Active participation in deliberative assemblies of the ancient polis
questions.explanation: Isaiah Berlin distinguished negative liberty ("freedom from external interference or coercion") from positive liberty ("freedom as self-mastery and rational self-direction").

questions.question_text: In Kautilya’s Arthashastra, the Saptanga Theory of the State enumerates seven constituent elements (Prakritis). Which element is identified as the "Janapada"?
questions.explanation: The seven limbs (Saptanga) in Kautilya’s Arthashastra are Swami (Ruler), Amatya (Minister), Janapada (Territory & Population), Durga (Fortified Capital), Kosha (Treasury), Danda (Army/Force), and Mitra (Ally).

questions.question_text: In his work "A Theory of Justice" (1971), John Rawls argues that the Difference Principle permits social and economic inequalities only if they:
questions.option_a: Maximize aggregate utility across the entire population regardless of distribution
questions.option_b: Work to the greatest benefit of the least-advantaged members of society
questions.option_c: Reward individuals strictly in proportion to aristocratic merit and lineage
questions.option_d: Eliminate all private ownership of productive assets through state nationalization
questions.explanation: John Rawls’s Second Principle of Justice includes the Difference Principle, which holds that inequalities are justifiable only if they are attached to offices open to all under fair equality of opportunity and work to the maximum benefit of the least-advantaged members of society.

questions.question_text: In Nyaya epistemology, which type of extraordinary perception (Alaukika Pratyaksha) enables the cognition of all members of a class through the perception of their shared universal (Samanya)?

questions.question_text: Which classical Indian school of philosophy upholds "Satkaryavada" in the specific form of "Parinamavada" (real transformation of cause into effect)?

questions.question_text: In his "Critique of Pure Reason", Immanuel Kant characterizes mathematical judgments such as "7 + 5 = 12" as:
questions.explanation: Kant argued that mathematical propositions amplify our knowledge (synthetic) because the concept of "12" is not merely contained by definition in "the sum of 7 and 5", yet they are universal and necessary (a priori).

questions.question_text: Jain epistemology expresses the relativity of conditional predication through seven-fold judgment known as:
questions.explanation: Syadvada (Saptabhangi Naya) is the Jaina doctrine of conditional predication consisting of seven modes prefixed with "Syat" (from a certain standpoint), grounded in Anekantavada (many-sidedness of reality).

questions.question_text: In propositional logic, the statement "(p ⊃ q) ≡ (~q ⊃ ~p)" represents which logical equivalence rule?
questions.explanation: Transposition (Contraposition) states that a conditional statement "if p then q" is logically equivalent to its contrapositive "if not-q then not-p".

questions.question_text: In propositional logic, the statement "(p ⊃ q) ≡ (~q ⊃ ~p)" represents which logical equivalence rule?
questions.explanation: Transposition (Contraposition) states that a conditional statement "if p then q" is logically equivalent to its contrapositive "if not-q then not-p".

questions.question_text: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz maintained that the fundamental, indivisible, windowless spiritual substances constituting reality are called:
questions.explanation: In "The Monadology" (1714), Leibniz argued that ultimate reality consists of an infinite hierarchy of simple, unextended, windowless substances called Monads, coordinated by God’s Pre-established Harmony.

questions.question_text: In Nyaya epistemology, which type of extraordinary perception (Alaukika Pratyaksha) enables the cognition of all members of a class through the perception of their shared universal (Samanya)?
questions.explanation: Samanyalakshana Pratyaksha is the extraordinary perception through which perceiving an individual possessing a universal (e.g., "cowness" in one cow) allows the cognizer to perceive all instances of that class in their generic character.

questions.question_text: Which classical Indian school of philosophy upholds "Satkaryavada" in the specific form of "Parinamavada" (real transformation of cause into effect)?
questions.explanation: Samkhya defends Prakriti-Parinamavada (a form of Satkaryavada), holding that the effect pre-exists in the material cause and undergoes a real transformation, unlike Advaita’s Vivartavada (apparent transformation).

questions.question_text: Damage to Wernicke’s area in the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere primarily results in:
questions.option_a: Non-fluent, effortful speech with intact comprehension

questions.option_d: Loss of motor coordination and balance (Ataxia)

questions.question_text: According to Harold Kelley’s Covariation Model of Attribution (1967), an observer attributes an actor’s behavior to an external (stimulus) cause when:
questions.option_a: Consensus is low, Distinctiveness is low, and Consistency is high

questions.option_c: Consensus is low, Distinctiveness is high, and Consistency is low
questions.option_d: Consensus is high, Distinctiveness is low, and Consistency is low
questions.explanation: In Kelley’s Covariation Model, when everyone reacts the same way (High Consensus), the actor reacts only to this specific stimulus (High Distinctiveness), and reacts every time (High Consistency), the behavior is attributed externally to the stimulus.

questions.question_text: In the Mughal Mansabdari system instituted by Emperor Akbar, the dual ranks "Zat" and "Sawar" denoted respectively:
questions.option_a: Hereditary land ownership and religious judicial authority

questions.option_c: Revenue collected from crown lands (Khalisa) and customs duties from ports
questions.option_d: Provincial governorship and command over artillery divisions
questions.explanation: Introduced in the 1570s and refined in the 1590s, "Zat" fixed the mansabdar’s personal rank and salary (talab-i-khass), whereas "Sawar" specified the contingent of horsemen (tabinan) he had to maintain.

questions.question_text: Who presided over the historic Lahore Session of the Indian National Congress in December 1929 that adopted the resolution of "Purna Swaraj" (Complete Independence)?

questions.question_text: In the IS-LM model for a closed economy, when the economy is caught in a Keynesian "Liquidity Trap" (horizontal LM curve), which policy is completely ineffective at raising equilibrium output?
questions.option_a: Expansionary Fiscal Policy through government expenditure
questions.option_b: Expansionary Monetary Policy through open market purchases
questions.option_c: Autonomous increase in public infrastructure investment
questions.explanation: In a Liquidity Trap, the interest elasticity of money demand is infinite, making the LM curve horizontal. Shifting the money supply does not lower the interest rate further, rendering Monetary Policy ineffective while Fiscal Policy achieves its full multiplier without crowding out.

questions.question_text: For a Cobb-Douglas production function Q = A · L^0.6 · K^0.6, the technology exhibits:
questions.option_a: Decreasing Returns to Scale (homogeneous of degree 0.6)
questions.option_b: Constant Returns to Scale (homogeneous of degree 1.0)
questions.option_c: Increasing Returns to Scale (homogeneous of degree 1.2)
questions.option_d: Zero Elasticity of Substitution between labor and capital
questions.explanation: In a Cobb-Douglas production function Q = A·L^α·K^β, the degree of homogeneity is α + β = 0.6 + 0.6 = 1.2 > 1, which implies Increasing Returns to Scale.

questions.question_text: According to the Stolper-Samuelson Theorem in the Heckscher-Ohlin international trade framework, an increase in the relative price of a commodity:
questions.option_a: Increases the real return to the factor used intensively in that commodity and decreases the real return to the other factor
questions.option_b: Equalizes nominal wages across countries regardless of transport costs
questions.option_c: Reduces the output of the commodity that uses the abundant factor intensively
questions.option_d: Leads to complete specialization under constant opportunity costs
questions.explanation: The Stolper-Samuelson Theorem demonstrates that under Heckscher-Ohlin assumptions, a rise in the relative price of a good raises the real reward (in terms of both goods) of the factor used intensively in its production and lowers the real reward of the other factor.

questions.question_text: In Classical Linear Regression (OLS), the violation of the assumption of constant error variance Var(u_i) = σ² across observations is known as:
questions.explanation: Heteroscedasticity occurs when the variance of the disturbance term u_i varies across observations. Under heteroscedasticity, OLS estimators remain unbiased and consistent, but they are no longer efficient (not BLUE) and standard errors are biased.

questions.question_text: For a Giffen good, which relationship between the Substitution Effect (SE) and Income Effect (IE) holds following a fall in its own price?
questions.option_a: Both SE and IE are positive, reinforcing quantity demanded
questions.option_b: The negative Income Effect is larger in magnitude than the positive Substitution Effect, causing quantity demanded to fall when price falls
questions.option_c: The Substitution Effect is zero because indifferences curves are L-shaped
questions.option_d: The Income Effect is zero because utility is quasi-linear
questions.explanation: A Giffen good is a strongly inferior good for which the negative income effect outweighs the substitution effect, resulting in an upward-sloping Marshallian demand curve.

questions.question_text: In the Solow-Swan neoclassical growth model with population growth rate (n), technological progress rate (g), and depreciation rate (δ), steady-state capital per effective worker k* satisfies:
questions.explanation: At the steady state in the Solow model with Harrod-neutral technological progress, actual investment per effective worker s·f(k*) equals break-even investment (n + g + δ)·k*.

questions.question_text: For a Giffen good, which relationship between the Substitution Effect (SE) and Income Effect (IE) holds following a fall in its own price?
questions.option_a: Both SE and IE are positive, reinforcing quantity demanded
questions.option_b: The negative Income Effect is larger in magnitude than the positive Substitution Effect, causing quantity demanded to fall when price falls
questions.option_c: The Substitution Effect is zero because indifferences curves are L-shaped
questions.option_d: The Income Effect is zero because utility is quasi-linear
questions.explanation: A Giffen good is a strongly inferior good for which the negative income effect outweighs the substitution effect, resulting in an upward-sloping Marshallian demand curve.

questions.question_text: In the Solow-Swan neoclassical growth model with population growth rate (n), technological progress rate (g), and depreciation rate (δ), steady-state capital per effective worker k* satisfies:
questions.explanation: At the steady state in the Solow model with Harrod-neutral technological progress, actual investment per effective worker s·f(k*) equals break-even investment (n + g + δ)·k*.

questions.question_text: In the IS-LM model for a closed economy, when the economy is caught in a Keynesian "Liquidity Trap" (horizontal LM curve), which policy is completely ineffective at raising equilibrium output?
questions.option_a: Expansionary Fiscal Policy through government expenditure
questions.option_b: Expansionary Monetary Policy through open market purchases
questions.option_c: Autonomous increase in public infrastructure investment
questions.explanation: In a Liquidity Trap, the interest elasticity of money demand is infinite, making the LM curve horizontal. Shifting the money supply does not lower the interest rate further, rendering Monetary Policy ineffective while Fiscal Policy achieves its full multiplier without crowding out.

questions.question_text: For a Cobb-Douglas production function Q = A · L^0.6 · K^0.6, the technology exhibits:
questions.option_a: Decreasing Returns to Scale (homogeneous of degree 0.6)
questions.option_b: Constant Returns to Scale (homogeneous of degree 1.0)
questions.option_c: Increasing Returns to Scale (homogeneous of degree 1.2)
questions.option_d: Zero Elasticity of Substitution between labor and capital
questions.explanation: In a Cobb-Douglas production function Q = A·L^α·K^β, the degree of homogeneity is α + β = 0.6 + 0.6 = 1.2 > 1, which implies Increasing Returns to Scale.

questions.question_text: According to the Stolper-Samuelson Theorem in the Heckscher-Ohlin international trade framework, an increase in the relative price of a commodity:
questions.option_a: Increases the real return to the factor used intensively in that commodity and decreases the real return to the other factor
questions.option_b: Equalizes nominal wages across countries regardless of transport costs
questions.option_c: Reduces the output of the commodity that uses the abundant factor intensively
questions.option_d: Leads to complete specialization under constant opportunity costs
questions.explanation: The Stolper-Samuelson Theorem demonstrates that under Heckscher-Ohlin assumptions, a rise in the relative price of a good raises the real reward (in terms of both goods) of the factor used intensively in its production and lowers the real reward of the other factor.

questions.question_text: In Walter Christaller’s Central Place Theory (1933), the K = 4 hierarchy of nested hexagonal market areas corresponds to which organizing principle?
questions.explanation: Christaller identified three principles: Marketing Principle (K = 3), Traffic/Transport Principle (K = 4, where lower-order centers lie at the midpoints of transport routes connecting higher-order centers), and Administrative Principle (K = 7).

questions.question_text: According to W.M. Davis’s "Geographical Cycle of Erosion" (1899), landscape evolution is a function of which "Trio of Davis"?
questions.option_c: Uplift Rate, Denudation Rate, and Slope Retreat
questions.explanation: William Morris Davis postulated that landforms are a function of Structure (lithology and tectonics), Process (geomorphic agents), and Stage (youth, maturity, old age culminating in a peneplain).

questions.question_text: In Köppen’s empirical classification of world climates, the code "Am" represents which climatic type found along the Western Coastal Plains (Konkan and Malabar) of India?
questions.option_a: Tropical Wet and Dry Savanna Climate
questions.option_b: Tropical Monsoon Climate with a short dry season
questions.option_c: Humid Subtropical Climate with dry winters
questions.explanation: In Köppen’s classification, "Am" denotes the Tropical Monsoon climate characterized by heavy monsoon rainfall that compensates for a short dry season, typical of India’s Malabar and Konkan coasts.

questions.question_text: Halford Mackinder’s 1904 and 1919 Geopolitical Heartland Thesis famously declared that whoever rules Eastern Europe commands the:
questions.option_b: Heartland (Pivot Area), and whoever rules the Heartland commands the World-Island
questions.explanation: Halford Mackinder formulated the dictum: "Who rules East Europe commands the Heartland; who rules the Heartland commands the World-Island; who rules the World-Island commands the world."

questions.question_text: In Remote Sensing, the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) is calculated using reflectance values from which two spectral bands?
questions.option_b: Near-Infrared (NIR) and Red (R) bands: (NIR - R) / (NIR + R)
questions.explanation: Healthy green vegetation strongly absorbs visible Red light (for chlorophyll photosynthesis) and strongly reflects Near-Infrared (NIR) radiation due to spongy mesophyll cell structure; hence NDVI = (NIR - Red) / (NIR + Red).

questions.question_text: Which ocean current is a cold eastern boundary current flowing northward along the western coast of South America, associated with ENSO variability when weakened?
questions.explanation: The Humboldt (Peru) Current is a cold, low-salinity ocean current flowing north along the west coast of South America; its periodic weakening and warming is the hallmark of El Niño events.

questions.explanation: Halford Mackinder formulated the dictum: "Who rules East Europe commands the Heartland; who rules the Heartland commands the World-Island; who rules the World-Island commands the world."

questions.question_text: In Remote Sensing, the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) is calculated using reflectance values from which two spectral bands?
questions.option_b: Near-Infrared (NIR) and Red (R) bands: (NIR - R) / (NIR + R)
questions.explanation: Healthy green vegetation strongly absorbs visible Red light (for chlorophyll photosynthesis) and strongly reflects Near-Infrared (NIR) radiation due to spongy mesophyll cell structure; hence NDVI = (NIR - Red) / (NIR + Red).

questions.question_text: Which ocean current is a cold eastern boundary current flowing northward along the western coast of South America, associated with ENSO variability when weakened?
questions.explanation: The Humboldt (Peru) Current is a cold, low-salinity ocean current flowing north along the west coast of South America; its periodic weakening and warming is the hallmark of El Niño events.

questions.question_text: In Walter Christaller’s Central Place Theory (1933), the K = 4 hierarchy of nested hexagonal market areas corresponds to which organizing principle?
questions.explanation: Christaller identified three principles: Marketing Principle (K = 3), Traffic/Transport Principle (K = 4, where lower-order centers lie at the midpoints of transport routes connecting higher-order centers), and Administrative Principle (K = 7).

questions.question_text: According to W.M. Davis’s "Geographical Cycle of Erosion" (1899), landscape evolution is a function of which "Trio of Davis"?
questions.option_c: Uplift Rate, Denudation Rate, and Slope Retreat
questions.explanation: William Morris Davis postulated that landforms are a function of Structure (lithology and tectonics), Process (geomorphic agents), and Stage (youth, maturity, old age culminating in a peneplain).

questions.question_text: In Köppen’s empirical classification of world climates, the code "Am" represents which climatic type found along the Western Coastal Plains (Konkan and Malabar) of India?
questions.option_a: Tropical Wet and Dry Savanna Climate
questions.option_b: Tropical Monsoon Climate with a short dry season
questions.option_c: Humid Subtropical Climate with dry winters
questions.explanation: In Köppen’s classification, "Am" denotes the Tropical Monsoon climate characterized by heavy monsoon rainfall that compensates for a short dry season, typical of India’s Malabar and Konkan coasts.

questions.question_text: The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015–2030), adopted at the Third UN World Conference in Japan, outlines how many Priorities for Action and Global Targets?
questions.option_a: 3 Priorities for Action and 5 Global Targets
questions.option_b: 4 Priorities for Action and 7 Global Targets (A through G)
questions.option_c: 5 Priorities for Action and 10 Global Targets
questions.option_d: 8 Priorities for Action and 17 Sustainable Targets
questions.explanation: The Sendai Framework (2015–2030) sets 4 Priorities for Action (Understanding risk, Strengthening governance, Investing in DRR for resilience, Enhancing preparedness to "Build Back Better") and 7 Global Targets (A–G).

questions.question_text: Under the Disaster Management Act, 2005 of India, who serves as the ex-officio Chairperson of the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA)?
questions.explanation: Under Section 3(2) of the Disaster Management Act, 2005, the Prime Minister of India is the ex-officio Chairperson of the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), while the Chief Minister chairs the SDMA.

questions.question_text: According to the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS IS 1893: Part 1), India is currently classified into which four Seismic Zones?
questions.option_a: Zones I, II, III, and IV
questions.option_b: Zones II, III, IV, and V (after merging Zone I into Zone II)
questions.option_c: Zones A, B, C, and D
questions.option_d: Zones III, IV, V, and VI
questions.explanation: Following the 2002 revision of BIS IS 1893, the erstwhile Zone I was merged with Zone II, leaving four official seismic zones in India: Zone II (Low), Zone III (Moderate), Zone IV (Severe), and Zone V (Very Severe, including NE India, Kutch, Andaman & Nicobar, and parts of the Himalayas).

questions.question_text: Which organization under the Ministry of Earth Sciences operates the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre (ITEWC) located in Hyderabad?
questions.option_b: Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS)
questions.explanation: INCOIS (Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services) in Hyderabad operates the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre (ITEWC), providing real-time tsunami advisories for India and Indian Ocean Rim countries.

questions.question_text: In the standard conceptual disaster risk equation used by UNDRR, Disaster Risk (R) is expressed as a function of Hazard (H), Exposure (E), Vulnerability (V), and Coping Capacity (C) as:
questions.explanation: Disaster Risk increases with the intensity/probability of the Hazard (H), the Exposure of elements at risk (E), and their Vulnerability (V), and is inversely proportional to Coping and Adaptive Capacity (C): R = (H × E × V) / C.

questions.question_text: In emergency medical triage during a Mass Casualty Incident (MCI) using the START protocol, a "Red Tag" (Priority 1) signifies:
questions.option_a: Minor injuries ("walking wounded") requiring delayed outpatient care
questions.option_b: Immediate life-threatening injuries requiring urgent medical intervention for survival
questions.option_c: Deceased or expectant victims beyond available emergency resources
questions.option_d: Non-urgent injuries where treatment can safely wait 12 to 24 hours
questions.explanation: In START (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment), Red indicates Immediate (Priority 1) life-threatening but treatable conditions; Yellow indicates Delayed (Priority 2); Green indicates Minor (Priority 3); Black indicates Deceased/Expectant.

questions.explanation: INCOIS (Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services) in Hyderabad operates the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre (ITEWC), providing real-time tsunami advisories for India and Indian Ocean Rim countries.

questions.question_text: In the standard conceptual disaster risk equation used by UNDRR, Disaster Risk (R) is expressed as a function of Hazard (H), Exposure (E), Vulnerability (V), and Coping Capacity (C) as:
questions.explanation: Disaster Risk increases with the intensity/probability of the Hazard (H), the Exposure of elements at risk (E), and their Vulnerability (V), and is inversely proportional to Coping and Adaptive Capacity (C): R = (H × E × V) / C.

questions.question_text: In emergency medical triage during a Mass Casualty Incident (MCI) using the START protocol, a "Red Tag" (Priority 1) signifies:
questions.option_a: Minor injuries ("walking wounded") requiring delayed outpatient care
questions.option_b: Immediate life-threatening injuries requiring urgent medical intervention for survival
questions.option_c: Deceased or expectant victims beyond available emergency resources
questions.option_d: Non-urgent injuries where treatment can safely wait 12 to 24 hours
questions.explanation: In START (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment), Red indicates Immediate (Priority 1) life-threatening but treatable conditions; Yellow indicates Delayed (Priority 2); Green indicates Minor (Priority 3); Black indicates Deceased/Expectant.

questions.question_text: [COQP08 Full-Length 1 · Q7] The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015–2030), adopted at the Third UN World Conference in Japan, outlines how many Priorities for Action and Global Targets?
questions.option_a: 3 Priorities for Action and 5 Global Targets
questions.option_b: 4 Priorities for Action and 7 Global Targets (A through G)
questions.option_c: 5 Priorities for Action and 10 Global Targets
questions.option_d: 8 Priorities for Action and 17 Sustainable Targets
questions.explanation: The Sendai Framework (2015–2030) sets 4 Priorities for Action (Understanding risk, Strengthening governance, Investing in DRR for resilience, Enhancing preparedness to "Build Back Better") and 7 Global Targets (A–G).

questions.question_text: [COQP08 Full-Length 1 · Q8] Under the Disaster Management Act, 2005 of India, who serves as the ex-officio Chairperson of the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA)?
questions.explanation: Under Section 3(2) of the Disaster Management Act, 2005, the Prime Minister of India is the ex-officio Chairperson of the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), while the Chief Minister chairs the SDMA.

questions.question_text: According to the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS IS 1893: Part 1), India is currently classified into which four Seismic Zones?
questions.option_a: Zones I, II, III, and IV
questions.option_b: Zones II, III, IV, and V (after merging Zone I into Zone II)
questions.option_c: Zones A, B, C, and D
questions.option_d: Zones III, IV, V, and VI
questions.explanation: Following the 2002 revision of BIS IS 1893, the erstwhile Zone I was merged with Zone II, leaving four official seismic zones in India: Zone II (Low), Zone III (Moderate), Zone IV (Severe), and Zone V (Very Severe, including NE India, Kutch, Andaman & Nicobar, and parts of the Himalayas).

questions.option_b: Zones II, III, IV, and V (after merging Zone I into Zone II)
questions.option_c: Zones A, B, C, and D
questions.option_d: Zones III, IV, V, and VI
questions.explanation: Following the 2002 revision of BIS IS 1893, the erstwhile Zone I was merged with Zone II, leaving four official seismic zones in India: Zone II (Low), Zone III (Moderate), Zone IV (Severe), and Zone V (Very Severe, including NE India, Kutch, Andaman & Nicobar, and parts of the Himalayas).

questions.question_text: Which organization under the Ministry of Earth Sciences operates the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre (ITEWC) located in Hyderabad?
questions.option_b: Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS)
questions.explanation: INCOIS (Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services) in Hyderabad operates the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre (ITEWC), providing real-time tsunami advisories for India and Indian Ocean Rim countries.

questions.question_text: In the standard conceptual disaster risk equation used by UNDRR, Disaster Risk (R) is expressed as a function of Hazard (H), Exposure (E), Vulnerability (V), and Coping Capacity (C) as:
questions.explanation: Disaster Risk increases with the intensity/probability of the Hazard (H), the Exposure of elements at risk (E), and their Vulnerability (V), and is inversely proportional to Coping and Adaptive Capacity (C): R = (H × E × V) / C.

questions.question_text: In emergency medical triage during a Mass Casualty Incident (MCI) using the START protocol, a "Red Tag" (Priority 1) signifies:
questions.option_a: Minor injuries ("walking wounded") requiring delayed outpatient care
questions.option_b: Immediate life-threatening injuries requiring urgent medical intervention for survival
questions.option_c: Deceased or expectant victims beyond available emergency resources
questions.option_d: Non-urgent injuries where treatment can safely wait 12 to 24 hours
questions.explanation: In START (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment), Red indicates Immediate (Priority 1) life-threatening but treatable conditions; Yellow indicates Delayed (Priority 2); Green indicates Minor (Priority 3); Black indicates Deceased/Expectant.

questions.question_text: [COQP08 Full-Length 8 · Q7] The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015–2030), adopted at the Third UN World Conference in Japan, outlines how many Priorities for Action and Global Targets?
questions.option_a: 3 Priorities for Action and 5 Global Targets
questions.option_b: 4 Priorities for Action and 7 Global Targets (A through G)
questions.option_c: 5 Priorities for Action and 10 Global Targets
questions.option_d: 8 Priorities for Action and 17 Sustainable Targets
questions.explanation: The Sendai Framework (2015–2030) sets 4 Priorities for Action (Understanding risk, Strengthening governance, Investing in DRR for resilience, Enhancing preparedness to "Build Back Better") and 7 Global Targets (A–G).

questions.question_text: [COQP08 Full-Length 8 · Q8] Under the Disaster Management Act, 2005 of India, who serves as the ex-officio Chairperson of the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA)?
questions.explanation: Under Section 3(2) of the Disaster Management Act, 2005, the Prime Minister of India is the ex-officio Chairperson of the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), while the Chief Minister chairs the SDMA.
